MPa, always ≤ 0. The part of water potential set by dissolved solutes. More solute, more negative.
MPa. Positive inside a living cell pressing on its wall. Negative in xylem under tension.
πo, osmotic potential at full turgor
MPa. Ψs of a fully hydrated cell. The main driver of the turgor loss point.
MPa. The water potential at which turgor reaches zero. Wilting is a visible symptom that may or may not follow.
MPa. Wall stiffness: turgor lost per unit fraction of cell water lost. Sets how much water a cell loses before turgor loss, and only nudges the potential.
%. Water held as a share of the water at full hydration.
kPa. The most water vapour air can hold at a given temperature. Roughly doubles every 11 to 12 °C.
kPa. How much vapour the air holds. Equals es at the dew point.
kPa. es − ea. The drying power of the air. Leaf to air VPD uses es at leaf temperature.
mm day⁻¹ or in month⁻¹. Water lost by a well-watered reference grass. Combines VPD, radiation, wind and temperature.
cm³ cm⁻³. Water volume per soil volume. The same θ can mean very different Ψsoil in sand and clay.
MPa. By convention −0.033 MPa (−0.01 for coarse soils): soil after free drainage.
MPa. By convention −1.5 MPa, from sunflower wilting (Richards and Weaver 1944). A convention, not a crop threshold.

mm per m of soil. Water held between field capacity and the wilting point convention, as a depth of water per depth of soil. Multiply by rooting depth for the size of the store. It depends on which field capacity you use, so it is a property of the method as much as of the soil.
van Genuchten, soil water retention curve
θ against MPa. θ(Ψ) = θr + (θs − θr) [1 + (αh)n]−m, m = 1 − 1/n. The same θ means very different Ψ in a sandy loam and a clay loam, and this equation is why.
m² leaf per m² ground. How much leaf a crop carries over each square metre of ground. It converts transpiration per unit leaf area into millimetres of water lost from the field.
mol m⁻² s⁻¹. How open the stomata are, as a conductance to water vapour.
mmol m⁻² s⁻¹. Water vapour leaving per leaf area per second. Roughly gs × VPD ÷ air pressure.
mmol m⁻² s⁻¹ MPa⁻¹. Flow per unit driving force. Flow = K × ΔΨ.
bundle sheath, the layer around a vein

One layer of cells wrapping each vein. Every molecule of water leaving the xylem crosses it, which makes it the gatekeeper between the vein and the mesophyll and the best current candidate for where leaf hydraulic conductance is controlled.
mmol m⁻² s⁻¹ MPa⁻¹. The part of leaf hydraulic conductance that is not the vein xylem: bundle sheath, living cells, walls and the air space. In many leaves it is the larger half, and it fails first.
Water moving in the cell walls and the spaces between cells, never crossing a membrane. In the leaf model it carries about 68 % of the flow outside the xylem.
symplastic, cell to cell through plasmodesmata
Water moving from one living cell to the next through the pores that join their cytoplasm, without crossing the plasma membrane.
Water crossing plasma membranes cell by cell, largely through aquaporins. About 19 % of the flow outside the xylem in the leaf model, and the route a plant can regulate fastest.
mmol m⁻² s⁻¹ MPa⁻¹. Conductance from petiole to evaporating sites, through xylem and then living cells.
%. 100 × (1 − K ÷ Kmax). What a vulnerability curve plots.
MPa. Xylem water potential at 12, 50 and 88 % PLC. With slope s at P50: P12 = P50 + 50/s, P88 = P50 − 50/s.
MPa. Seasonal minimum Ψ minus P50 (or P88). Small or negative means living close to failure.
Rapid formation of a gas void in water under tension.
A conduit filled with gas that no longer conducts water.
Air pulled through a pit membrane pore from an embolised conduit into a water-filled one. ΔP = 4T/D.
pit membrane, the sheet between two conduits
Where two conduits touch, the thick wall is missing and only a thin porous sheet is left. Water crosses it freely; air is meant not to.
pit aperture, the mouth of a pit
The opening on each side of a pit, where the wall arches over and leaves a gap into the conduit.
torus, the disc in a conifer pit
A thick solid patch in the middle of a conifer pit membrane. It has no pores, so nothing goes through it.
margo, the web around the torus
The open mesh of strands holding the torus in place, in conifers. Nearly all the water goes through this mesh, and the mesh also slows it down.
When the pressure on one side of a conifer pit is much lower, the torus is pushed across and plugs the opening. The gas-filled tracheid is then shut off from its neighbour.
A conduit breaks at its single leakiest pore, so a conduit with more pit membrane has more chances of owning a bad one and fails sooner.
MPa. The turgor a growing wall must exceed before it extends irreversibly. The cell can adjust it within minutes.
MPa⁻¹ h⁻¹. How fast the wall extends per MPa of turgor above Y.
MPa. Accumulating solutes so πo becomes more negative and turgor holds at more negative Ψ. In grapevine it follows the season.
A cell drying in air: wall and protoplast shrink together. Plasmolysis needs an outside solution: it happens in salt solutions and on slides, rarely in a drying leaf.
conduit, a vessel or a tracheid
One dead, hollow cell of the xylem that water moves through. In a grapevine petiole they are vessels. Dead is the normal state: it is what makes the tube.
lumen, the space inside a conduit or cell
The bore the wall encloses. The wall reads bright whatever the lumen holds; only the lumen's grey tells you water or gas.
pith, the centre of the petiole
A lattice of large, thin-walled living cells inside the ring of vascular bundles. Not xylem, and it is a region of its own.
A pith cell whose lumen reads dark because it holds gas, not water. Also called dry pith.
fibre cap, the bright block outboard of the phloem
Thick-walled fibres on the outer face of each bundle. Bright and dense right through, with no lumen to call.
Living cells filling the space between bundles and between the bundles and the epidermis. Thin walls, irregular shapes, no bright ring.
Small, thin-walled cells on the outer side of each bundle, between the xylem and the fibre cap. It sits like an eyebrow above the eye.
